The reason the stock fell from $30 to $20 is because analysts saw a product getting more expensive that no one wanted to pay more for.

What they really missed was that this isn't a hardware company as much a digital products company, but we'll get to that...

The memory crisis forced console price hikes consumers wouldn't pay. And they were right for the last year. Sony raised PS5 prices twice in 12 months and US unit sales in May fell 58%, the worst May for PlayStation since 2000.

Then GTA 6 pre-orders opened and the trailer dropped.

The PS5 Pro is now sold out at $900 three months early. Scalpers are getting $1,300. That's what demand inelasticity looks like.

$SONY's hardware economics just flipped.

For the past year they were discounting PS5s into weak demand. Last holiday's global promo crushed gaming margins and units still fell. In May, US PS5 sales hit their worst level since 2000.

Now every console they can build through the holidays is effectively pre-sold. Zero promo spend needed. Two price hikes stuck. Mix is shifting to the $900 Pro, and demand came back anyway.

Supply is capped by memory, so units won't grow. They don't need to. For the first time since launch Sony will sell every box at full price, hardware flips from breakeven to profitable, and every unit ships with an $80 copy of GTA, a PS Plus sub, and a 30% toll on years of micro-transactions.

And here's what the bears keep missing: consoles are only 20% of $SONY gaming revenue, and Sony sells them near breakeven. 73% of the segment is software and services:

$9B add-on content (Sony keeps ~30% of every micro-transaction)
$7B digital full games (same cut on every $80 GTA copy)
$5B PS Plus (required to play GTA Online)

The console was never the product. It's a digital storefront with 93M units installed, and on Nov 19 the biggest entertainment launch in history goes live inside it. Every copy, every Shark Card, every new PS Plus sub pays Sony a toll.

Despite this $SONY's current guide has gaming sales down yoy and the huge profit uplift guide is based on an impairment made on a studio from last year.

The company has a history of delivering a huge guidance revision in November, which marks half their fiscal year. That coincides with a week before game launch.

One of the less savory parts of being a defense investor is program timing, and this is a prime example. But NGSRI is $0 of current revenue and $0 of the $110M backlog.

Also there's a huge catalyst outside of this for $LPTH.

I asked Sam about the $820M Pentagon loan to Performance Drone Works and whether LightPath could get similar federal backing. His answer:

"There's multiple discussions on multiple angles... I don't know if it would be a loan or an equity or a grant. We are in discussion with multiple different vehicles like that inside the Department of War, and I'm pretty sure there's going to be something. I can't share what, but there will be."

That's the CEO saying government capital is coming, he just can't say what form.

Sam told me 75%+ of American drones already carry LightPath optics. If DoW is funding the domestic drone supply chain, the dominant US supplier of drone optics is an obvious candidate.

I see this sell off as overdone. If I do exit my trading position, it's not going to be today.

$KRKNF reported earnings today and I want to share my honest read through for investors.

Let's start with the numbers, which were mostly alligned with expectations. Also remember, this is just Kraken and not the much larger business, Covelya, they acquired in the spring, and the business is always back half weighted.

- Revenue C$27.3M, up 4% from C$26.4M. Slight miss. Without a C$1.5M one-time revenue reversal C$28.8M and up 9%.

- Net loss of C$7.5M. C$6.9M of that is a one-time arbitration charge. Adjusted EBITDA was C$5.0M, up 7%.

- Guidance unchanged: C$290M to C$320M revenue, C$65M to C$75M adjusted EBITDA, with half a year of Covelya in it. Good.

Margins expanded nicely, customer diversification is happening into more programs, and new product opps in seabed sentry were highlighted. Greg also highlighted that customers are not making batteries in-house. Hormuz tailwind will be huge long term for their business. 

But here's what I didn't like:

My original thesis for $KRKNF was the best public proxy for Anduril. That's my focus. It appears that Anduril isn't ready for full scale production, so Kraken is talking to more customers. If Kraken trusted that Anduril's ramp was around the corner, they wouldn't be diversifying the customer base.

There was no mention of a U.S. factory. A U.S. factory would be a clear signal Kraken is getting ready for Anduril's ramp.

Greg did not offer timing on the CAMP program from the U.S. Navy, which is currently testing 3/4 subs using Kraken batteries. That's bullish, but again, no timeline given.

Also what's frustrating is not one word on the TSX uplisting. Not in the release, not on the call, and no analyst asked. Last we heard was July 2: end of 2026 or early 2027. 

It makes no sense why Kraken is still trading on the TSX-V. It should at the minimum be on the TSX and honestly the NASDAQ, and management dragging their feet here is not good. Kraken needs majority institutional ownership and more volume so it can move with other drone/defense names/high beta.

Overall it looks like the Anduril ramp is going to take longer than anticipated, which is why I highlighted in past posts for what I'm waiting for to get excited again.

It may be worth getting aggressive on the stock again when a US Navy contract gets announced for Anduril, or another program outside of Australia of size. 

Don't get me wrong, Kraken is an excellent business, with a high barrier to entry, competent management, right in the middle of a supercycle, with a real multi-bagger set up long term.

I still think it hits its asymmetrical ramp with Anduril, just not this year. What we want to own is an Anduril proxy scaling with the next $1T defense company. I think it happens, but it may be a 2027 story so it's worth calling out depending on your time horizon as an investor (looking for near term opportunities versus just sticking with a high quality idea through vol).

With where we're at with late stage capitalism and rise of AI, high inflation + interest rates feels like it's going to be the normal for a very long time.

Because even if we were to go back to tightening rates, AI is SO asymmetrical, how can we as investors possibly treat the future cash flows of businesses like we did in the past?

The whole point of a discount rate is that a dollar five years out is worth less than a dollar today. Rates go up, that far off dollar is less attractive. That math obviously hurts stocks.

But that lesson assumes the future dollars stay roughly the same size while the discount rate eats them. What if the future dollars are 3x, 5x, 10x bigger than anyone modeled because of AI. 

I mean look at the earnings growth we're seeing now across the board, and this revolution hasn't even started yet.

I'm sure a negative macro could send markets sideways, maybe down a bit near term, but the long term picture of how much some of these companies are going to grow is going to make the discount rate look like a rounding error.

I recently sat down with the CEO of a $900M drone components stock supplying Anduril.

Overall, the defense trade has been miserable in 2026, despite a record budget, a war that exposed huge capability gaps, and an administration that's all in.

While we've seen a modest recovery recently. Many of retail's favorite drone and defense plays are still down massively off their ATHs. 

So I wanted to share with retail investors invested in drones about what I learned about the defense supercycle after speaking to someone on the ground floor of this, Sam Rubin of $LPTH.

1) On why defense stocks have been so weak since the Iran war, Sam's read is that sentiment and the numbers have completely decoupled. Europe is rebuilding armies from scratch and blowing past the 2% GDP target Trump was asking for. Add the munitions burned in the Gulf that have to be replaced before anyone preps for the next theater. He expects his own business to double every 12 months as a norm.

2) Investors pile into AI infrastructure because trillions are being spent. Defense budgets are also trillions and the market refuses to treat them the same way. Sam's bullish distinction is arguing that what he sells is a consumable. A missile gets fired once. A bomb gets dropped once. That isn't a one off capex cycle, it repeats for years.

3) The lock-in is what nobody prices correctly. Getting designed into a program takes forever. Approvals, qualification, testing. But once you're in, you're in for a decade plus foreign military sales and aftermarket on top. The Stinger ran 40 years before anyone designed a replacement. A data center might see its chips/equipment be obsolete in a matter of a few years or less. 

4) The drone manufacturing layer itself gets commoditized. Sam agreed the barrier to entry is very low, and once the US component base is onshored you can assemble one in a garage. Ukraine proved that. The value doesn't accrue to whoever stamps out the airframe. It accrues to whoever owns the critical component piece nobody else can make.

5) China export controls are only ramping up. Thermal imaging runs on germanium, China controls supply, and it's a byproduct metal so you can't just mine more. The US is now closing the door on it for defense optics. Every incumbent built their cameras around a material they can no longer use. Physical input, hostile supplier, regulatory deadline.

6) Last thing and it's the constraint across this entire trade. He authorized capex he can't deploy because equipment lead times blew out. Defense onshoring is now competing for the same equipment and skilled labor as the data center buildout. The money is appropriated. The capacity to absorb it isn't there.

I recently sat down with a $4.5B critical metals CEO. Here's what I learned.

It's been a strong week for mining stocks, especially after the market got a reminder of the long game the Trump Admin is playing with another $3B in commitments. 

But overall, many rare earth / mining stocks have underperformed heavily this year, even despite a massive rally in high beta stocks after the Iran ceasefire.

$TMC: -42.3% YTD
$LAC: -27.8% YTD
$TMQ: -13.2% YTD
$NB: -9.3% YTD
$CRML: -5.3% YTD

So I thought it'd be interesting to share my takeaways from interviewing Lewis Black, CEO of Tungsten miner $ALM about the overall sector and of course Tungsten specifically.

1) As for the sector's underperformance, Lewis attributed it to the "dreaded junior miner". Basically there's been a surge in mining companies, without any operating mines, getting funding or hype in the last year based on all the Trump funding. You need to find companies with real operating mines, growing revenue and profits, with management teams invested alongside. If there's no permits, it is a multi-year, long story...

2) Why should retail care about critical metals at all? Because there's no AI without them. His analogy was that you can bake the greatest cake in the world but not without wheat. Every semiconductor on earth needs tungsten gas during fabrication, tiny amounts, zero substitutes. The AI trade has run through chips, then memory, now power. Almost nobody is pricing the raw inputs sitting underneath all of it.

3) Permitting and processing are where the real moat lives, not in the ground. He's watched an enormous amount of capital get destroyed in this space, and his read is that basically every mine outside his own in Tungsten that has tried to open has failed, because processing is the hard part. That's the part promoters skip. The ore body is the easy story to sell. Turning it into product that a customer will actually take is where projects die.

4) The best geopolitical filter I heard all year. Someone gave Lewis this framework and he passed it on. When you're assessing a critical metals project, ask whether in the event of World War Three it would still supply the United States. That single question kills most of the map. It's why a lot of headline projects in jurisdictions everyone is excited about right now don't clear the bar.

5) The bigger picture is China moving downstream, and it applies to the whole complex. Defense demand is about to pull hard on supply that doesn't exist yet, and something has to give. Lewis's bet is that less essential sectors like autos lose access first, and Europe would rather accept Chinese finished components than slow their lines. China spent 30 years selling the West cheap raw material. Now they take the value-add layer. That's the shift investors should be positioning around, not just the spot price of any one metal.

Tim paid $50,000 for a potential 10x payout ($500,000) if California doesn't fix the issue. So basically business insurance through a hedge, ensuring he'll survive the delay.

TLDR: $LASR stock is down 35% after a weak guide on uncertain procurement of Chinese optical components.

The CEO attributed it to what appears to be China increasing scrutiny on dual-use products for defense tech. He has no timeline either when they'll be back and wasn't specific about what exactly these products were. 

"The particular commodity that I would highlight would be optics. These are not specialized components. They're materials where China has built out an outsized portion of the overall supply chain over time."

On June 18, 2026 a Chinese precision optics company  disclosed that its chairman had been placed under compulsory measures by Shanghai Customs anti-smuggling. The alleged violation: declaring exported lenses containing germanium as ordinary optical glass to get around export licensing. So suppliers are on edge.

I don't think there's a big read through into datacom optics from this - $LITE, $COHR, $AAOI. In my view, Chinese is getting most aggressive on defense linked optical products. This was already in motion with a Germanium ban, which is needed for IR sensors for drones, and we've seen escalating actions there for months.

$LASR's diodes run around 900nm on gallium arsenide  while lasers from $LITE $COHR $AAOI are Indium phosphide. From my rather limited research, it doesn't appear there's many shared components from $LASR's products with data center optics. InP has already been under Chinese export control since February 2025 and its well documented/understood as a chokepoint.

That being said if there is some kind of Chinese transceiver ban from the U.S. (rumored) we could potentially see tighter InP export controls in return from China if U.S. targets their domestic photonics companies like Innolight and Eptolink, which would have a negative impact.

For now looks to be defense focused but this optical war with China needs to be watched.

I found the most fascinating divergence in global macro.

The most recent South Korean consumer sentiment reading sits above 100, meaning optimists outnumber pessimists, and has held near multi-year highs. 

Meanwhile U.S. consumer sentiment is at its lowest on record. 

So why does one country feel rich and the other feel broke? Both countries saw their stock markets rip to record highs this year. 

The KOSPI is up 57% compared to the S&P at just 9.5% YTD, that could explain it. But it's not necessarily the returns that create the divergence.

It's HOW citizens in each country own stocks.

Korea has 105 million active brokerage accounts in a country of 51 million people. Retail is roughly half of all trading volume. Margin debt just hit an all time high of 38.5 trillion won. Samsung and SK Hynix alone account for 51% of daily market turnover, and once you add the single stock leverage and inverse ETFs, it clears 80%.

Koreans don't have "exposure" to the market. They ARE the market. Direct, concentrated, levered. The KOSPI doubled in 9 months and every kitchen table in Seoul FELT it. That's your consumer sentiment print.

America is the opposite. 58% of families own stock but only 21% picked individual stocks, and that ownership number has been flat near 20% for three decades. The percentage of Americans trying to make multi-bagger returns is a tiny fraction of Koreans. 

Because of this, Americans have exposure to the markets but don't really feel it. They glance at a quarterly 401k statement moving up with the index and go back to paying for gas. They're not building an active trading strategy around thematics or speculating on AI bottlenecks.

Fable 5 tells me only about half of Americans might recognize Nvidia by name, even less could tell you what it does. Meanwhile, 99% of Korean people know their largest companies like Samsung and SK Hynix intimatley.

Of course, it's likely that the next consumer sentiment reading in Korea will be markedly lower after the country's stock market has fallen 20% in just the last month. Leverage, speculation, and active trading around a couple of companies is a two way street.

But certainly a fascinating difference between two economies at the center of the AI revolution.

$ERII makes a special piece of tech that makes desalination plants economical. The PX Pressure Exchanger recycles the pressure inside a seawater reverse osmosis plant and cuts its energy use by up to 60%. This hero product accounts for over 90% of $ERII's revenue and commands gross margins over 60%. 

I love $ERII because it feels like a high margin IP business, not a low margin industrial, despite being priced like one.

So why is the stock trading half off its February $16 price and a fraction of its comps?

The Middle East, the world's largest desalination market, is 50% of their revenue. And two huge gut punches nuked the stock across two ER's.

1) Revised 26 guidance down before the Iran War started.
2) Removed 26 guidance entirely during the War due to the massive ME concentration of business. Then the CEO and CFO both left.

But the business isn't broken. And the Iran War looks to be resolved, making more signals of sustained ME peace a real catalyst.

Q1 is their smallest quarter historically and revenue still grew 20% YoY. The ugly Q1 loss was a one time charge from killing their CO2 side project. Q4'25 was a record $66.9M at 67% gross margin.

The balance sheet is a fortress too. $77M net cash, almost  no debt, a 9x current ratio, ~$27M TTM FCF, and they buy back stock at a ~9% yield. You get paid to wait and this is not a small cap where you get diluted.

The tailwinds are massive for $ERII's desalination business and I think the market may be mispricing $ERII's growth potential on 4 vectors.

1) Fast Growing Market

Water scarcity isn't a regional story anymore, it's a global one. Rivers and aquifers are drying up while population, industry, and now AI all pull harder on the same shrinking supply, and desalination is the backstop the world keeps falling back on. Reverse osmosis dominates new capacity, every RO plant needs an energy recovery device, and the PX is the standard, so $ERII's installed base scales as desal scales globally.

2) Water As Warfare

The Iran war turned water into a weapon. Plants got hit across Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE and Iran, and with desal supplying up to 90% of water in some Gulf states, every ministry just learned a centralized, aging fleet is a strategic weak spot. The answer isn't to build less. It's to harden, decentralize, and build MORE, which means more PX sales.

3) Middle East AI

Every gigawatt of compute landing in the Gulf has to be cooled, and up to 90% of the region's water comes from desal, so water is the constraint of where you can build. PwC sees Gulf data center capacity tripling to ~3.3GW by 2030, all running through RO where $ERII sells the picks and shovels. Management isn't even telling this story yet, but when they bring in a new permanent CEO, I could see him pushing AI + water scarcity angle.

4) AI Factory Wastewater Upside

This one is early but $ERII just carved wastewater out as its own segment, it's ~6% of revenue today. It's the OTHER end of the AI water story: data centers and the chip fabs feeding them discharge dirty water and the laws require treatment before it leaves. ERII uses the same PX tech here with same 60% margin profile, and management expects this to get bigger in 2027.

Five hard lessons I've learned about stocks.

1) Worship volume and liquidity. Even if you find better fundamentals on a foreign exchange, in most cases, the U.S. listed equivalent is the better play.

3) Forget sizing big into binary stocks (mining, biotech, buyouts). The opportunity cost is way too high when a catalyst has no clear time frame. Investors are impatient and they're so quick to ditch a stock when it takes longer than expected.

It's not dilution and it is not guaranteed selling of any amount, it is just the shadow of known future supply that weighs on price discovery.

Firefly Aerospace is a misunderstood space stock trading 35% off its ATH with an extremely unique set of assets.

Here's why I think this $6B space pioneer is an asymmetrical bet.

I love $FLY because its business spans the full orbital stack: roughly 20% launch, 40% spacecraft, and 40% defense software.

On the spacecraft side, $FLY’s Blue Ghost lander makes it the only company in history to land successfully on the moon. A 10 year old space startup achieved the same feat only 5 countries had before. It now has $487M in contracted NASA missions and CEO Jason Kim has said Firefly is in discussions with NASA about block buy contracts for 5 to 10 landers, which would represent between $500 million and $1.4 billion in a single order. That’s asymmetric growth against a company doing $160 million in trailing revenue.

$FLY also has a spacecraft called Elytra which is this swiss army knife of sorts. It’s part tugboat, part sentinel. It launches payloads, deploys them, then stays on station for years as a comms relay, surveillance platform, or deployer. What I love about Elytra is that it’s about to monopolize lunar imaging using Nvidia Jetson compute which can create high-margin revenue to map mining and landing sites as we work to colonize the moon.

Now the real leverage with $FLY is that it also builds its own rockets. It has a small lift rocket called Alpha that’s done seven launches (it’s worth noting only 3 were successful, but $RKLB’s first Electron flights were also rocky) and has a medium lift rocket Eclipse launching in early 2027 co-developed with Northrup Grumman. This timeline isn’t too far off $RKLB’s delayed Neutron vehicle now Q4 2026.

The key point here is that Firefly’s spacecraft will one day own the highway on which they travel. As the launch business progresses, it’s de-risked by hundreds of millions worth of lunar landing contracts, helping boost margins on the primary spacecraft division. Vertical integration at its finest.

Don’t get me wrong, $FLY is significantly behind its comparable $RKLB in the launch market. It’s a Ford to a Ferrari. But here's what many retail investors interested in space need to understand. 

Space companies like $RKLB and SpaceX are not being priced on their launch businesses as much as they are their higher margin divisions. $RKLB’s premium multiple is justified by their space systems division and specifically the components business (60-70% gross margins) or with SpaceX, Starlink.

That’s where $FLY’s defense software becomes so important. I think it’s the primary vector on which the market is mispricing Firefly.

Firefly bought a missile defense AI software company called SciTec in November that brought $164M in trailing revenue, about equal to $FLY’s entire 2025 haul and about 40% of 2026 guidance in an accretive transaction that was mostly stock at $50/share. This business is EBITDA and cash flow positive, a rarity in any space economy unit. It has a $372M FORGE contract with the Space Force and has major upside with the $185B Golden Dome initiative.

If 40% of $FLY’s revenue is coming from an extremely fast growing Palantir-esque defense software company with margins that are presumably much higher than anything Rocket Lab is doing in space systems…

Then why should $FLY trade at such a steep discount to $RKLB? Just 12.5x forward EV/Revenue compared to 43x for $RKLB. I think as the market better grasps the SciTec opportunity, we could see $FLY re-rate to at least half of $RKLB’s multiple, presenting major upside over the current share price.

Of course there are massive risks with this idea. $FLY isn’t expected to deliver positive EPS until 2028, while comps like $RKLB and $LUNR are expected to do so in 2027. Over $800M in cash is a decent war chest but dilution will happen as the company has maxed out its credit facility, so investors should be prepared for ATMs.

A shitty launch record with Alpha doesn’t instill major confidence for the launch business or the future synergies of that business on the rest of the pie, but it's still early and RKLB electron had early stage issues too. Launch commoditization is a risk here but it's mitigated by the massive pipeline of NASA lunar lander contracts if Eclipse can service some of those payloads. Private equity company AE industrial partners is also a big governance risk, with 3 board seats and majority voting control. They forced a bad acquisition on $RDW, which diluted shareholders. Finally, there’s just massive execution risks in any space business that can lead to significant delays combined with lumpy government contracting revenue that can lead to earnings misses.

Overall, I think $FLY is the most complete small cap space package that the market is still sleeping on. It owns the moon, the rockets, and the software. And if the SpaceX IPO is supposed to re-rate the entire space sector, isn’t $FLY the biggest direct beneficiary since the mission is now the Moon and not Mars? It’s the space stock most primed to directly assist SpaceX with its primary IPO objective.

This couple made $85M copying Starbucks. 

Now they make $400M/yr copying Chipotle.

In the 80’s, Seattle became the epicenter of American coffee culture.

it’s why Scott and Ally Svenson were so homesick when they left Washington to live in London.

People in the UK were mainly tea drinkers which meant a good cup of coffee was hard to come by.

So they started Seattle Coffee Company in 1993.

It was modeled almost exactly off of Starbucks, except for the fact, that it was based in England.

Scott and Ally faced an uphill battle to educate British people about coffee blends and the American order to-go culture.

But they quickly expanded from one store to dozens across England.

When Starbucks set its sights on the UK, it made more sense for CEO Howard Shultz to buy Scott and Ally’s chain than to start from scratch.

After pocketing $85M from the deal, the Svenson’s saw another opportunity years later.

Chipotle and Subway let diners customize burritos and sandwiches and get served in minutes.

But that didn’t exist for Pizza.

So the couple created Made on Demand Pizza aka MOD Pizza in 2010 becoming the first fast-food chain in Pizza.

In 2019, MOD became America’s fastest growing restaurant chain and revenues exceeded $400M.

These college kids built a a $50M tutoring app that's destroying Chegg.

Few startups have world-class distribution AND product. 

@kadama has both.

The company's core insight?

If you can drive people around in a car to make spare cash, why not help a freshman with Calculus 101?

Amin Shaykho, Marwan El-Rukby, and Dani Shaykho are the co-founders of Kadama.

In early 2020, at University of Washington, they had an idea to connect students with tutors in the traditional sense–physically on campus.

But when COVID hit, the trio was forced to think bigger.

It birthed a disruptive thought: why does tutoring need to be geography based?

What if students, anywhere in the world, could be connected instantly to the best possible tutor by clicking a button?

If a student in CA is procrastinating at 11 PM (which most do), they should be connected to a tutor in Australia where it's daytime.

This insight birthed Kadama or in other words the "Uber for tutoring".

As the team started to build the first app version for Kadama, the co-founders also spotted the rise of TikTok.

Their ingenius short-form video marketing, in the form of ultra-viral "life-hack" videos that subtly feature their product or loosely link to its value prop has driven over 2M followers.

Very few companies have brilliant marketing and exceptional product.

Kadama has both.

Not only did they build with an insanely cheap cost of customer acquisition but their tech chops saw them ship improvements and A/B test the app with lightning speed to make users happy.

Fast forward to today and Kadama has 2M users and thousands of tutors around the world making a living from their platform.

Going forward, the Kadama boys are raising their Series A as they look to add more AI features and take down industry giants in the edtech space.

With $5M in revenue and on track for $10M next year, they're off to the races.

This entrepreneur built a $50M company by age 25 selling heavy blankets.
 
@AaronSpivak2 notices a crazy stat in 2017. 

Search terms for weighted blankets: 300,000.

Stressed adults have huge WTP for a better sleep.

He and his co-founder dove in head first 🛏️

Task 1: solve for the quality issues they were noticing in the market (like length - not covering people's toes).

After naming their company Hush and selling their first batch, a problem became clear.

While people found weighted blankets helpful for sleep...

They were too hot to support a comfortable rest.

So Aaron went back to the drawing board and designed an iced fabric.

It helped people attain the benefits of weighted blankets *without the excessive warmth*.

This product put Hush on a rocket ship.

It went from $600K in year 1 to $10M in year 2.

But Aaron had no intention of competing with other weighted blanket manafacturers.

Him being hyper-attentive to competition is an understatement.

Aaron claimed that he knew "the rent of his competitors," and exactly the margin he could beat them at.

His larger vision was to create the ultra-premium brand in the category, untouchable by other companies.

Part of this brand-first strategy included Aaron and Lior's appearance on Dragon's Den, Canada's version of Shark Tank.

They draped the dragons in their sleep gear and won the "most epic pitch" award for that season.

By 2021, Hush became Canada's fastest growing sleep brand.

The co-founders took their company's reputation for world-class sleep quality and extended it into products like sheets, mattresses, and pillows.

A majority stake in Hush was acquired at a $48M valuation in 2021, around three years after Aaron and Lior started the company.

Copy his business model in the next emerging sport. Think cricket or UFC.

This high school dropout from Alabama sold his startup to Target for $550m.

San Francisco isn't always the right place to start a tech company.

He escaped competition from Instacart by conquering the American south. 

Bill left high school because he was making $5k/mo selling cell phones to small businesses.

What he later realized though, is the frequency at which people buy groceries is far greater than any other product.

After telling his 10 engineers that they could quit or help him pivot to same-day grocery delivery...

They all stayed on.

An advantage behind Bill’s company Shipt is where he built it.

If you start a new app in a tech-friendly place like SF, the odds it’s relevant to the rest of America are uncertain.

That’s why starting in Alabama was so crucial.

Bill grew Shipt to tens of millions in sales by focusing on the American South.

It shielded Shipt from competition by Instacart, which was well-capitalized and conquered wealthier cities like Seattle and SF.

In 2017, Target bought Shipt for $550M.

Part of Bill’s negotiations was that Target had to keep Shipt’s headquarters in Alabama.

Today, Garret is a father and husband, and he even found a way to make a business out of that.

This guy made billions becoming the world’s biggest patent troll.

Nathan Myhrvold is a polymath genius and Microsoft’s former CTO.

Now he runs one of the most peculiar insurance firms.

How?

By holding 30,000+ software patents.

In the late 90’s, U.S. courts were making it easier for people to get patents on software

Here's where it gets interesting.

Most software patents are super broad and their meaning can be vaguely applied.

There’s high potential that every tech company is using some version of all the software patents.

It’s why Nathan raised $5B to start Intellectual Ventures.

He bought over 30,000 patents in the software industry.

Because of this vast portfolio...

He goes to massive companies and charges them huge fees in exchange for an agreement that he won’t sue them.

As Nathan began to mass purchase patents, so did the big companies.

The more patents you hold, the more protection you have against being sued.

It's essentially mutually assured destruction if someone else sues you.

American tech companies spend billions buying patents every year for this reason.

And Nathan is by far the biggest winner.
